questions.q: How does Linux organize storage compared to Windows's C:\ and D:\ drive letters?
options: Identically — Linux also assigns letters to each disk
There is a single root directory, and other devices are mounted onto folders inside that one tree
Linux has no concept of multiple storage devices
Each user account gets its own separate root directory
questions.explain: Linux uses one single-rooted tree starting at /. Additional disks or devices are mounted onto a folder within that tree rather than getting a separate drive letter.

questions.q: Where would you expect to find system-wide configuration files on any standard Linux distribution?
options: /etc
/tmp
/dev
/proc
questions.explain: /etc is the FHS-standard location for system-wide configuration files, which is why configuration management tools target it specifically.

questions.q: What does the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) actually guarantee?
options: That every distribution uses the same package manager
That the purpose of major top-level directories like /etc and /var is consistent across distributions
That every Linux server has identical installed software
That root is the only user account allowed to exist
questions.explain: The FHS standardizes what each major directory is for (e.g., /etc for config, /var for runtime data), not the specific software installed or user accounts present.

questions.q: On a modern Ubuntu system, what does `ls -la /` reveal about `bin` and `sbin`?
options: They are empty, unused directories
They are symlinks pointing into /usr/bin and /usr/sbin
They only exist on RHEL-based systems
They contain user home directories
questions.explain: Modern Ubuntu merged /bin and /sbin into /usr, leaving symlinks at the old paths so existing scripts and habits referencing /bin or /sbin keep working.

questions.q: Why does a deployment script install an in-house application under /opt rather than scattering its files elsewhere?
options: /opt is reserved exclusively for the Linux kernel
/opt is the FHS convention for self-contained applications installed outside the distro's package manager
/opt is the only writable directory on a Linux system
/opt is a synonym for /tmp
questions.explain: /opt exists specifically as a predictable, standard home for third-party or in-house software that doesn't come through the distribution's own package manager.
